prime.problem: Before this paper, generated code was graded by how much its text resembled a reference answer. That says nothing about whether the code runs, so nobody could say how good a language model really was at programming.
prime.fits: The map for the whole deck. Every later card is one link in a single pipeline: train on GitHub Python, specialise on task-shaped problems, sample many programs, grade them by running tests, then name what still goes wrong.
expect: functional correctness scored by unit tests
the paper's own limitations: chaining, misalignment
prime.goal: Draw the paper's causal map from corpus to benchmark number, and say which card explains each link and each limitation.

attend: Which decision in the pipeline changed what the reported numbers mean, rather than how high they are?
Why does going from 1 sample to 100 lift Codex-S-12B from 37.7% to 77.5%, and what hidden assumption makes that jump fair to report?
What does the gap between 77.5% (oracle over 100) and 44.5% (mean log-prob pick of 100) tell you about deploying this model without tests?
GPT-3 scores 0% and Codex-12B 28.8%. Which two stages between them explain the gap, and which one only makes training cheaper?
Which of the listed limitations would get better with a bigger model, and which does the paper say get worse?

must: Text-overlap metrics can't tell a working program from a near-copy with one flipped operator → grade by running unit tests (functional correctness) → needs hand-written, uncontaminated problems (HumanEval) and a sandbox to run untrusted code → pass@k becomes the headline number

Code is judged by tests, not taste → many independent samples + a filter beats one careful sample → pass@k rises with k and the best temperature rises with it → but only an oracle (tests) can pick the winner, so without tests you fall back to ranking by mean log-probability

GitHub Python is mostly not 'docstring → function' → a second fine-tune on ~50k task-shaped problems (Codex-S) → better pass@k at every size, but a narrower distribution that needs a higher temperature for diversity

The model continues its prompt rather than following intent → long chained docstrings decay roughly 2–3× per step and buggy context yields buggier code → these limits are about specification and alignment, not raw scale
elevated: pass@k is estimated from n = 200 samples with an unbiased formula, evaluated in a numerically stable product form → numbers are comparable across papers that sampled different amounts, and the estimator never overflows
reference: the abstract's 70.2% vs Table 1's 72.31% pass@100 for Codex-12B

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the paper as one causal map: corpus → models → sampling → grading → metric, with a side branch for limitations. Label each box with the card that explains it, then write one sentence on why the metric choice matters more than any single model number.
checklist: fine-tune GPT on GitHub Python → Codex; fine-tune again on curated, test-verified problems → Codex-S
sample many programs (temperature + top-p 0.95), run them in a sandbox against HumanEval's unit tests
report pass@k with the unbiased estimator; rank by mean log-probability when there are no tests
BLEU is rejected because it can't separate correct from wrong samples
limitations: sample inefficiency, docstring chaining decay, intent misalignment

retrieve.q: Explain why this paper had to build a new benchmark instead of scoring Codex on existing code datasets with BLEU.
answer: BLEU scores text overlap, and correct and wrong samples overlap in BLEU
scraped GitHub or Codeforces problems are likely in the training data
hand-written problems with unit tests measure correctness without contamination

retrieve.q: Walk one HumanEval problem through the whole pipeline: from the prompt the model sees to the number that lands in pass@100.
answer: the model gets the signature and docstring
200 bodies are sampled at the chosen temperature inside a 0.95 nucleus
each runs in a gVisor sandbox against the problem's unit tests; c of them pass
pass@100 for that problem = 1 − C(200−c,100)/C(200,100); the reported figure averages over 164 problems

retrieve.q: A product team wants to ship Codex-S-12B as an autocomplete that shows one suggestion. Which of the paper's headline numbers should they quote, and why not the most impressive one?
answer: not pass@100 (77.5%): it assumes an oracle picks the passing sample
one shown suggestion is pass@1 (37.7%), or 44.5% if they rank 100 samples by mean log-probability
ranking costs 100 generations per suggestion

retrieve.q: Which of the paper's limitations would you expect to shrink with scale, and which does the evidence say does not?
answer: loss falls smoothly with size, and pass@k rises with it
the misalignment gap on buggy prompts grows with size
insecure-crypto suggestions show no robust size trend
chaining decay is only measured on Codex-12B, so its size trend is open

compare.q: Both papers grade code by running tests on HumanEval. What does EvalPlus claim this paper got wrong, and which design choice here makes that possible?
answer: here: an average of 7.7 hand-written tests per problem
EvalPlus: weak tests let wrong programs pass, so pass@k is inflated
the root cause is that functional correctness is only as good as the test suite, which this paper flags but doesn't fix

compare.q: Structured outputs guarantee a valid shape; Codex's tests check behaviour. Map each paper's 'correct' onto the other's: what does each one's guarantee leave unchecked?
answer: a schema mask guarantees parseable output, not correct values
unit tests check behaviour on the tested inputs only
both need a separate check for what their guarantee doesn't cover

predict.q: Suppose the authors had kept BLEU as the headline metric and still trained Codex-S. Would Codex-S's gain over Codex have been visible, hidden, or possibly reversed? Commit, then reveal.
predict.answer: Possibly hidden or even reversed. Codex-S learns to write bodies that work for docstring-shaped tasks, not bodies that textually match a reference. Correct programs with a different algorithm score near 0 BLEU, and near-copies with one flipped operator score high, so a metric that can't separate the two can't reliably see a gain in correctness either.

apply.task: Design scenario: you have 5 candidate programs per problem and no unit tests, only the model's token log-probs. Using only numbers from this deck, write a one-paragraph evaluation plan saying (1) which metric you can honestly report, (2) how you'd pick one program to show a user, and (3) what you'd need to add before you could report pass@5.
apply.done: Your plan names pass@1 or ranked-pick accuracy as the honest number, picks by mean (not summed) log-probability, and says pass@5 needs an oracle: unit tests run in a sandbox, plus the unbiased estimator if you ever sample more than 5.
apply.hint: The paper reports 44.5% for mean-log-prob ranking of 100 Codex-S samples against 37.7% for a random one, and says ranking by sum can be worse than random.
